title: Writing to inform
keyIdea: Writing to inform means telling a reader true facts about one topic. An information text names the topic first, often with a heading and a first sentence like "Frogs live in and near ponds." Then it gives facts, keeps every sentence on the topic and leaves out feelings and made-up bits. Labels on a picture are facts too. A closing sentence sums up, instead of "The end."

kid: Some writing tells a story. Some writing tells true facts. When you write to inform, you tell a reader facts about one topic, like frogs or bees.
Start by naming the topic. Put a heading at the top, like "Frogs". Then write a first sentence: "Frogs live in and near ponds." Now the reader knows what your page is about.
Next, write facts. A fact is true. "Tadpoles grow into frogs" is a fact. "I think frogs are cute" is a feeling, so leave it out. Every sentence must be about frogs.

You can draw a picture and add labels, like "wing" or "leg". Each label points to its part. At the end, write a closing sentence, like "Now you know how frogs grow." Do not write "The end." That is for stories.
adult: In the English National Curriculum, Year 1 and Year 2 pupils write for different purposes, including non-fiction, and sequence sentences to form short texts. US Common Core W.K.2 and W.1.2 ask children to write informative or explanatory texts. They name a topic, supply some facts and provide some sense of closure. Drawing and dictating count at the start.

An information text has a heading, an opening sentence that names the topic, a few facts, and often a labelled picture. It ends with a closing sentence. Children also learn what to leave out: opinions ('the best', 'I think'), made-up details and sentences about something else.

Common mistakes: drifting into a story ('Once upon a time a frog…'), ending with 'The end.', mixing in feelings as if they were facts, and adding a sentence about the writer's day. Labels on the wrong part are a slip too. Be careful not to mark a child down for spelling at this stage. The aim is facts in a clear order, said aloud or written.

In the lab your child picks first sentences that name a topic, sorts frog sentences into facts and not-facts, and taps the off-topic sentence on two pages. They label a butterfly's wing, antenna, body and leg. Then they build a frog page in order: heading, topic sentence, two facts and a closing sentence.

familyTip: Pick something your child knows well, like how to brush teeth or what the dog eats. Ask them to tell you three facts while you write them down, then read it back and ask: is every sentence about the topic? How shall we finish?

visual.caption: Information or story? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Once upon a time a bee met a king.
The dragon flew over the hill.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: name the topic, sort facts from feelings, cut the off-topic sentence, label a butterfly and build an information page in order.

practice.prompt: Which is the best first sentence for a page about bees?
choices: Bees are insects that make honey.
Once upon a time there was a bee.
practice.hint: Which one tells the reader the topic?
practice.explain: "Bees are insects that make honey" names the topic and gives a fact. The others are a story and something else.

practice.prompt: Sam writes {n} facts about cats and one closing sentence. How many sentences is that?
practice.hint: Add the closing sentence to the facts.
practice.explain: {n} facts and 1 closing sentence make {=n+1} sentences.

choices: My dog can drive a car.
practice.hint: A fact is true for every dog.
practice.explain: Dogs have four legs is true. "The best" is a feeling, and a dog driving is made up.

practice.prompt: A page about frogs has {n} sentences. One says "I had cake." How many sentences are about frogs?
practice.hint: Take away the sentence that is not about frogs.
practice.explain: {n} take away the cake sentence leaves {=n-1} sentences about frogs. Cut the cake one!

pool.prompt: How should an information page end?
choices: Now you know how bees live.
pool.hint: Stories end with "The end." What does information do?
pool.explain: A closing sentence sums up the topic. "The end" is for stories.

pool.hint: The heading tells you the topic first.
pool.explain: The heading goes at the top, so the reader knows the topic before the facts.

pool.prompt: Which sentence does not belong on a page about fish?
choices: My brother has a red coat.
pool.hint: Which sentence is not about fish?
pool.explain: The coat sentence is about something else. The other two are fish facts.

pool.prompt: "I think owls are pretty." What is it?
pool.explain: "I think" tells a feeling. A fact is true for everyone.

pool.prompt: You draw a butterfly and add {n} labels. Then you add 1 more label for the legs. How many labels now?
A label says "wing". Where should it point?
pool.hint: Labels point to the part they name.
pool.explain: A label points to its own part, so "wing" points to the wing.

pool.prompt: Mia writes {n} sentences about trains. {k} of them are about her lunch. How many are about trains?
pool.explain: {n} take away {k} lunch sentences leaves {=n-k} sentences about trains.

choices: How to make a jam sandwich
pool.hint: Which one tells true facts or steps?
pool.explain: Steps for a jam sandwich tell true things. The dragon story and the poem do not inform.
